correctness.rationale: For an anisotropic nondegenerate form, every subspace is nondegenerate, so the kernel/image orthogonal decompositions give a Moore–Penrose inverse for every endomorphism. Conversely, from any nonzero isotropic vector the audited rank-one construction gives elements with zero first triple product and a nonzero transposed product whose image is an isotropic line; such an operator cannot possess a Moore–Penrose inverse because its range would be the range of a self-adjoint idempotent and hence nondegenerate. This proves the zero-triple condition, full transfer condition, anisotropy, and star-regularity equivalence. For transpose over a finite field, the standard quadratic form is anisotropic only in dimension one or in dimension two when the field order is congruent to three modulo four; the dimension-at-least-three case follows from the standard finite-field quadratic-form zero argument.

originality.rationale: The 2026 motivating paper asks the Moore–Penrose transposed-triple question but does not state the adjoint-ring classification in its accessible primary abstract. Resultary returned the assigned record as the exact match. Older work of Pearl and Huylebrouck–Puystjens–Van Geel concerns existence of Moore–Penrose inverses over arbitrary fields and semisimple Artinian rings; the accessible primary abstracts do not state that the transposed-triple property is equivalent to anisotropy of the defining Hermitian form. The unavailable full texts are retained as residual risk rather than treated as evidence of novelty.

value.rationale: The theorem gives a structural answer to the source question on a canonical large class of rings with involution, identifies the exact geometric obstruction, and yields a concrete finite-field classification. It is more than a renamed standard inverse criterion because the zero-triple transfer property is shown to detect anisotropy.
